codes.title: Continue
codes.short_description: Request received, continue sending the rest.
codes.description: The server has received the request headers and the client should proceed to send the request body. This is used to avoid sending a large request body before the server checks if the request is valid.
when_to_use: Client wants server approval before sending body

example_response.message: Continue

codes.best_practice: Always check for 100-continue expectation headers before sending large payloads.

codes.title: Switching Protocols
codes.short_description: Server is switching protocols as requested.
codes.description: The server understands and is willing to comply with the client's request to switch protocols. The Upgrade header field in the response indicates the protocol(s) to which the server is switching.

example_response.message: Switching Protocols

codes.best_practice: Use WebSocket upgrade via 101 for real-time, bidirectional communication instead of polling.

codes.title: Processing
codes.short_description: Server is processing the request (WebDAV).
codes.description: An interim response used to inform the client that the server has accepted the complete request but has not yet completed it. Primarily used in WebDAV to prevent the client from timing out.
when_to_use: File operations taking more than 20 seconds

example_response.message: Processing

codes.best_practice: Send 102 every 10-15 seconds for long operations to keep the connection alive.

codes.title: Early Hints
codes.short_description: Returns preliminary headers before final response.
codes.description: Used to return some response headers before the final HTTP message. Allows the user agent to start preloading resources while the server is still preparing a response.

example_response.message: Early Hints

codes.best_practice: Use 103 with Link headers to dramatically improve page load performance by preloading critical assets.

categories.title: 2xx Success
categories.description: Request was successfully received, understood, and accepted.

codes.title: OK
codes.short_description: Request succeeded. Standard response for successful requests.
codes.description: The standard success response. The actual response will depend on the request method used. In a GET request, the response will contain an entity corresponding to the requested resource. In a POST request, the response will contain the result of the action.
when_to_use: POST requests that create or update

example_response.message: OK

codes.best_practice: Always include the resource representation in a 200 response body. Return consistent response envelopes across your API.

codes.title: Created
codes.short_description: Resource created successfully.
codes.description: The request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created. The newly created resource can be referenced by the URI(s) returned in the entity of the response, with the most specific URI given by a Location header.
when_to_use: POST requests that create a new resource

example_response.message: Created

codes.best_practice: Always return the Location header pointing to the new resource, and include the created object in the response body.

codes.title: Accepted
codes.short_description: Request accepted for processing, not yet completed.
codes.description: The request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed. The request might or might not be eventually acted upon, and may be disallowed when processing occurs.

example_response.message: Accepted

codes.best_practice: Always return a job ID and a polling URL so the client can check the status of the asynchronous operation.

codes.title: Non-Authoritative Information
codes.short_description: Response from a third-party or transformed proxy.
codes.description: The server is a transforming proxy that received a 200 OK from its origin but is returning a modified version of the origin's response.

example_response.message: Non-Authoritative Information

codes.best_practice: Include a Warning header to help clients understand the response was transformed.

codes.title: No Content
codes.short_description: Request succeeded, no content to return.
codes.description: The server has successfully fulfilled the request and there is no additional content to send in the response payload body. Usually returned as a response to a DELETE or update operation.
when_to_use: PATCH/PUT updates that don't need a response body

example_response.message: No Content

codes.best_practice: Use 204 instead of 200 with an empty body for DELETE operations. Never include a body with a 204 response.

codes.title: Reset Content
codes.short_description: Client should reset the document view.
codes.description: The server has fulfilled the request and desires that the user agent reset the document view, which caused the request to be sent, to its original state as received from the origin server.
when_to_use: After submitting a form that should be cleared
Clearing a canvas or editor after save

example_response.message: Reset Content

codes.best_practice: Use 205 when you want the client to clear its form or input fields after a successful operation. Do not include a response body.

codes.title: Partial Content
codes.short_description: Server is sending only part of the resource (range request).
codes.description: The server is delivering only part of the resource due to a Range header sent by the client. Used by HTTP clients to enable resuming of interrupted downloads, or to split a download into multiple streams.
when_to_use: Large file downloads with resume support

example_response.message: Partial Content

codes.best_practice: Always support Range requests for any endpoint serving large files or media to enable efficient streaming and resumable downloads.

codes.title: Multi-Status
codes.short_description: Multiple status codes for multiple operations (WebDAV).
codes.description: Conveys information about multiple resources in situations where multiple status codes might be appropriate. This response is used in WebDAV to communicate results of multiple operations on multiple resources.
when_to_use: Bulk API responses with mixed results

example_response.message: Multi-Status

codes.best_practice: Use 207 for batch APIs where each sub-operation can independently succeed or fail. Always include individual status codes per item.

codes.title: Already Reported
codes.short_description: DAV bindings already enumerated in a previous reply.
codes.description: Used inside a DAV: propstat response element to avoid enumerating the internal members of multiple bindings to the same collection repeatedly. It means the resource has already been listed in a previous response.
when_to_use: Avoiding duplicate entries in multi-status responses
Circular reference detection in WebDAV collections

example_response.message: Already Reported

codes.best_practice: Only relevant in WebDAV. Ensure your WebDAV server correctly tracks already-reported bindings to avoid infinite loops.

codes.title: IM Used
codes.short_description: Server fulfilled GET using instance manipulations.
codes.description: The server has fulfilled a GET request for the resource, and the response is a representation of the result of one or more instance-manipulations applied to the current instance. Used for HTTP Delta encoding.

example_response.message: IM Used

codes.best_practice: Only use 226 when you implement full HTTP Delta encoding (RFC 3229). Not widely supported by clients — prefer other bandwidth optimizations.

categories.title: 3xx Redirection
categories.description: Further action needs to be taken in order to complete the request.

codes.title: Multiple Choices
codes.short_description: Multiple options available for the requested resource.
codes.description: The request has more than one possible response. The user agent or user should choose one of them. There is no standardized way of choosing one of the responses, but HTML links to the possibilities are recommended.

example_response.message: Multiple Choices

codes.best_practice: Provide a clear list of alternatives with their content types. Prefer content negotiation via Accept headers over 300 responses.

codes.title: Moved Permanently
codes.short_description: Resource permanently moved to a new URL.
codes.description: The URL of the requested resource has been changed permanently. The new URL is given in the response. Search engines update their links and browsers cache this redirect, so future requests go directly to the new URL.

example_response.message: Moved Permanently

codes.best_practice: Use 301 only when the move is truly permanent. After issuing a 301, the old URL should be kept handling redirects indefinitely.

codes.title: Found
codes.short_description: Resource temporarily resides at a different URL.
codes.description: The target resource resides temporarily under a different URI. Since the redirection might be altered on occasion, the client ought to continue to use the effective request URI for future requests.

example_response.message: Found

codes.best_practice: Use 302 for temporary redirects. For POST requests, use 303 See Other to redirect to a GET request after form submission.

codes.title: See Other
codes.short_description: Redirect to another URI with a GET request.
codes.description: The server is redirecting the user agent to a different resource, indicated by a URI in the Location header, which is intended to provide an indirect response to the original request. The redirected request MUST use GET method.
when_to_use: After a successful POST to redirect to a result page
After form submission to a confirmation page

example_response.message: See Other

codes.best_practice: Always use 303 (not 302) after a POST form submission to implement the Post/Redirect/Get pattern and prevent duplicate submissions on refresh.

codes.title: Not Modified
codes.short_description: Resource not modified since last request (cached version valid).
codes.description: Indicates that the resource has not been modified since the version specified by the request headers If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match. The client should continue to use the cached version of the response.

example_response.message: Not Modified

codes.best_practice: Always implement ETags and Last-Modified headers. Proper cache validation via 304 can reduce bandwidth by 80%+.

codes.title: Use Proxy
codes.short_description: Requested resource must be accessed through a proxy (deprecated).
codes.description: The requested resource must be accessed through the proxy given by the Location field. The Location field gives the URI of the proxy. This status code is deprecated due to security concerns.

example_response.message: Use Proxy

codes.best_practice: Do NOT use 305. It is deprecated and removed from HTTP/1.1 spec due to security concerns. Use network-level proxy configuration instead.

codes.title: Temporary Redirect
codes.short_description: Resource temporarily at another URL; same HTTP method must be used.
codes.description: The target resource resides temporarily under a different URI and the user agent MUST NOT change the request method if it performs an automatic redirection to that URI. Unlike 302, 307 guarantees the method and body is preserved.
when_to_use: Temporary server-side redirects where POST must be preserved
Maintenance pages that must preserve POST data

example_response.message: Temporary Redirect

codes.best_practice: Prefer 307 over 302 when you want to temporarily redirect but need to ensure the HTTP method (POST, PUT) is preserved.

codes.title: Permanent Redirect
codes.short_description: Resource permanently moved; same HTTP method must be used.
codes.description: The target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs. Like 307, it preserves the HTTP method and body.

example_response.message: Permanent Redirect

codes.best_practice: Use 308 instead of 301 when you need clients to re-send the entire request (body and method) to the new URL permanently.

categories.title: 4xx Client Errors
categories.description: The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled.

codes.title: Bad Request
codes.short_description: Server cannot process request due to client error.
codes.description: The server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error such as malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing.

example_response.message: Validation failed

codes.best_practice: Always return detailed validation errors with the specific field names and error messages. Never return a generic 400 without explanation.

codes.title: Unauthorized
codes.short_description: Authentication required or has failed.
codes.description: The client request has not been completed because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the requested resource. The server must send a WWW-Authenticate header with a challenge. Despite the name, this is about authentication, not authorization.

example_response.message: Invalid or expired authentication token

codes.best_practice: Return 401 for authentication failures, not 403. Always include the WWW-Authenticate header. Use short-lived tokens and refresh token patterns.

codes.title: Payment Required
codes.short_description: Payment required to access this resource.
codes.description: Originally reserved for future use in digital payment systems. Now used by some APIs to indicate that the user's payment is required (subscription expired, credit limit reached, etc.).
when_to_use: API quota exhausted and paid upgrade is needed

example_response.message: Your subscription has expired. Upgrade to continue.

codes.best_practice: While non-standard, 402 is increasingly used for billing-related blocks. Always include an upgrade or payment URL in the response body.

codes.title: Forbidden
codes.short_description: Server refuses to authorize the request.
codes.description: The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it. Unlike 401 Unauthorized, the client's identity is known but they don't have permission to access the resource. Re-authentication will make no difference.
when_to_use: User is authenticated but lacks permissions

example_response.message: You do not have permission to access this resource

codes.best_practice: Return 403 (not 401) when the user is authenticated but unauthorized. Consider returning 404 instead to not reveal the resource exists.

codes.title: Not Found
codes.short_description: Requested resource could not be found.
codes.description: The server cannot find the requested resource. Links that lead to a 404 page are often called broken or dead links. A 404 status code only indicates that the resource is missing; it does not indicate whether the absence is temporary or permanent.

example_response.message: User with ID 999 was not found

codes.best_practice: Implement proper 404 pages. Use 404 (not 403) to hide existence of private resources. Log 404s to catch broken links.

codes.title: Method Not Allowed
codes.short_description: HTTP method is not supported for this resource.
codes.description: The request method is known by the server but is not supported by the target resource. The server MUST generate an Allow header field containing a list of the target resource's currently supported methods.

example_response.message: GET is not allowed on this endpoint

codes.best_practice: Always include the Allow header listing supported methods. If your framework doesn't do this automatically, add it manually.

codes.title: Not Acceptable
codes.short_description: Server cannot produce a response matching the Accept headers.
codes.description: The server cannot produce a response matching the list of acceptable values defined in the request's proactive content negotiation headers, and the server is unwilling to supply a default representation.
when_to_use: Client requests XML but API only serves JSON

example_response.message: Cannot produce response in application/xml

codes.best_practice: Always document your API's supported content types. Return available formats in the error response.

codes.title: Proxy Authentication Required
codes.short_description: Client must authenticate itself with the proxy.
codes.description: The client must first authenticate itself with the proxy. The proxy must return a Proxy-Authenticate header containing a challenge applicable to the requested resource.

example_response.message: Please authenticate with the corporate proxy

codes.best_practice: Use proper proxy authentication. For modern architectures, avoid placing auth proxies in front of APIs; use API Gateway auth directly.

codes.title: Request Timeout
codes.short_description: Server timed out waiting for the request.
codes.description: The server did not receive a complete request message within the time it was prepared to wait. The client may repeat the request without modifications at any later time.
when_to_use: Client never sent the request body

example_response.message: The server closed the connection after waiting 30 seconds

codes.best_practice: Configure appropriate server read timeouts. Return 408 to free up server resources. The client should implement retry logic with exponential backoff.

codes.title: Conflict
codes.short_description: Request conflicts with the current state of the resource.
codes.description: The request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource. This code is used in situations where the user might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request.

example_response.message: A user with this email already exists

codes.best_practice: Use optimistic locking with ETag/version numbers to detect conflicts. Return the conflicting resource's current state so the client can merge changes.

codes.title: Gone
codes.short_description: Resource permanently deleted and will not return.
codes.description: The target resource is no longer available at the origin server and that this condition is likely to be permanent. If you don't know whether the condition is temporary or permanent, use 404 instead.

example_response.message: This resource has been permanently deleted

codes.best_practice: Use 410 over 404 for intentionally deleted resources. Search engines will de-index 410 pages faster than 404 pages.

codes.title: Length Required
codes.short_description: Content-Length header is required but not provided.
codes.description: The server refuses to accept the request without a defined Content-Length. The client MAY repeat the request if it adds a valid Content-Length header field containing the length of the message body in the request message.
when_to_use: Streaming requests to servers requiring length

example_response.message: Content-Length header is required

codes.best_practice: Configure your server to require Content-Length for POST requests. Most HTTP clients add this automatically.

codes.title: Precondition Failed
codes.short_description: Precondition specified in request headers evaluated to false.
codes.description: One or more conditions given in the request header fields evaluated to false when tested on the server. This response code allows the client to place preconditions on the current resource state to prevent the request from being applied if the resource has been modified.

example_response.message: ETag mismatch. Resource was modified by another client.

codes.best_practice: Use If-Match with ETags for safe concurrent updates. Always return the current ETag in the 412 response so the client can re-fetch and merge.

codes.title: Content Too Large
codes.short_description: Request body exceeds server's size limit.
codes.description: The server is refusing to process a request because the request payload is larger than the server is willing or able to process. The server may close the connection to prevent the client from continuing the request.
when_to_use: Batch operations with too many items

example_response.message: Maximum request size is 10MB

codes.best_practice: Implement chunked uploads for large files. Always specify and document your maximum request size. Return the limit in the error response.

codes.title: URI Too Long
codes.short_description: Request URI is longer than the server can process.
codes.description: The server is refusing to service the request because the request-target is longer than the server is willing to interpret. This rare condition is only likely to occur when a client has improperly converted a POST request to a GET request with long query information.
when_to_use: Improperly encoded large data in URL
GET requests with too many parameters

example_response.message: Request URI exceeds the maximum allowed length of 8192 characters

codes.best_practice: Move large data from query strings to the request body using POST. Keep URLs under 2000 characters for maximum browser/server compatibility.

codes.title: Unsupported Media Type
codes.short_description: Request's media type is not supported by the server.
codes.description: The origin server is refusing to service the request because the payload is in a format not supported by this method on the target resource. The format problem might be due to the Content-Type or Content-Encoding.
when_to_use: Sending XML to a JSON-only API

example_response.message: Only application/json is supported

codes.best_practice: Clearly document accepted content types. Return the list of supported types in the error response.

codes.title: Range Not Satisfiable
codes.short_description: Server cannot serve the requested byte range.
codes.description: The server cannot serve the requested ranges. The most likely reason is that the document doesn't contain such ranges, or that the Range header value, though syntactically correct, doesn't make sense.
when_to_use: Requesting byte ranges that don't exist

example_response.message: The requested range is not satisfiable

codes.best_practice: Always return a Content-Range header with the actual resource size in a 416 response so the client can adjust its range request.

codes.title: Expectation Failed
codes.short_description: Server cannot meet the requirement in the Expect header.
codes.description: The expectation given in the Expect request header field could not be met by at least one inbound server. This is often triggered when the client sends Expect: 100-continue but the server cannot fulfill the expectation.

example_response.message: Server does not support 100-continue

codes.best_practice: If you control both client and server, disable Expect headers for small requests. Only use 100-continue for genuinely large request bodies.

codes.title: I'm a Teapot
codes.short_description: Server refuses to brew coffee with a teapot (April Fools).
codes.description: The HTTP 418 I'm a Teapot client error response code indicates that the server refuses to brew coffee because it is, permanently, a teapot. This code was defined as an April Fools' joke in RFC 2324 (Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol).

example_response.message: I refuse to brew coffee. I am a teapot.

codes.best_practice: Don't use in production. Some developers use 418 for bot detection, but this is non-standard. For joke endpoints it's fine.

codes.title: Misdirected Request
codes.short_description: Request directed at a server that cannot produce a response.
codes.description: The request was directed at a server that is not able to produce a response. This can be sent by a server that is not configured to produce responses for the combination of scheme and authority included in the request URI.
when_to_use: HTTP/2 connection reuse with wrong server
Request routed to wrong virtual host

example_response.message: This server cannot produce a response for the requested host

codes.best_practice: Ensure your HTTP/2 connection pooling respects server certificates. Implement proper SNI handling in reverse proxies.

codes.title: Unprocessable Entity
codes.short_description: Request well-formed but semantically incorrect.
codes.description: The server understands the content type of the request entity and the syntax of the request entity is correct, but it was unable to process the contained instructions. Used for semantic validation errors where the request is syntactically valid.
when_to_use: Valid JSON with invalid business logic

example_response.message: Validation failed

errors.message: Start date cannot be in the past

codes.best_practice: Use 422 for semantic errors (business logic), not 400 (syntax errors). Provide field-level errors for form validation.

codes.title: Locked
codes.short_description: Resource being accessed is locked (WebDAV).
codes.description: The source or destination resource of a method is locked. This response should contain an appropriate precondition or postcondition code, such as lock-token-submitted or no-conflicting-lock.
when_to_use: WebDAV resource locked by another client
Preventing concurrent edits on a document

example_response.message: The resource is currently locked by another user

codes.best_practice: Always include lock expiry time and the lock holder identity in your response. Implement lock timeouts to prevent deadlocks.

codes.title: Failed Dependency
codes.short_description: Request failed due to a failure of a previous request (WebDAV).
codes.description: The method could not be performed on the resource because the requested action depended on another action and that action failed. For example, if a command in a PROPPATCH method fails, then, at minimum, the rest of the commands will also fail with 424.
when_to_use: WebDAV batch operation with failed dependency
Transaction rollback due to dependent failure

example_response.message: Resource creation failed because the parent resource does not exist

codes.best_practice: In batch APIs, clearly indicate which dependency failed and what needs to be resolved first.

codes.title: Too Early
codes.short_description: Server is unwilling to process a request that might be replayed.
codes.description: Indicates that the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed. This is used to prevent replay attacks with early data in TLS 1.3 handshakes.

example_response.message: Server will not process 0-RTT early data

codes.best_practice: Return 425 for non-idempotent requests sent as TLS 1.3 early data. Safe (GET, HEAD) requests can be allowed; unsafe (POST, DELETE) should be rejected.

codes.title: Upgrade Required
codes.short_description: Client must switch to a different protocol.
codes.description: The server refuses to perform the request using the current protocol but will be willing to do so after the client upgrades to a different protocol. The server sends an Upgrade header to indicate the required protocol(s).

example_response.message: Please upgrade to HTTPS

codes.best_practice: Always redirect HTTP to HTTPS at the infrastructure level. Use HSTS headers to prevent future plain-HTTP requests.

codes.title: Precondition Required
codes.short_description: Server requires the request to be conditional.
codes.description: The origin server requires the request to be conditional. This response is intended to prevent the 'lost update' problem, where a client GETs a resource's state, modifies it, and PUTs it back to the server, when meanwhile a third party has modified the state on the server.

example_response.message: An If-Match or If-Unmodified-Since header is required for this request

codes.best_practice: Return 428 on PUT/PATCH/DELETE endpoints to enforce clients to always include an If-Match header. Prevent accidental overwrites in concurrent scenarios.

codes.title: Too Many Requests
codes.short_description: Client has sent too many requests (rate limiting).
codes.description: The user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time (rate limiting). The response should include details explaining the condition and may include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait.

example_response.message: Rate limit exceeded. Max 100 requests per minute.

codes.best_practice: Always include Retry-After header. Use token bucket algorithms. Communicate rate limits via X-RateLimit headers on every response.

codes.title: Request Header Fields Too Large
codes.short_description: Request headers are too large for server to process.
codes.description: The server is unwilling to process the request because its header fields are too large. The request may be resubmitted after reducing the size of the request header fields. It can be used both to indicate that the overall header size, or a specific header field, is too large.
when_to_use: Too many or too large cookies

example_response.message: Request headers exceed the maximum allowed size of 8KB

codes.best_practice: Keep cookies and headers small. Use token references (IDs) instead of storing large data in cookies. Reduce custom header count.

codes.title: Unavailable For Legal Reasons
codes.short_description: Resource unavailable due to legal demands.
codes.description: The server is denying access to the resource as a consequence of a legal demand. The server in question might not be an origin server. This status code is named after the Ray Bradbury novel Fahrenheit 451.

example_response.message: This content has been removed following a DMCA takedown notice

codes.best_practice: Include a link to the legal notice or court order where permitted. Be transparent about what authority issued the demand when legally allowed.

categories.title: 5xx Server Errors
categories.description: The server failed to fulfil a valid request.

codes.title: Internal Server Error
codes.short_description: Unexpected server error occurred.
codes.description: The server encountered an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request. This is a generic error message when no more specific message is suitable. The server should minimize the information it reveals to the client.

example_response.message: An unexpected error occurred

codes.best_practice: Never expose stack traces or internal details to clients. Log everything server-side with a correlation ID. Return that ID so users can report issues.

codes.title: Not Implemented
codes.short_description: Server does not support the requested functionality.
codes.description: The server does not support the functionality required to fulfill the request. This is the appropriate response when the server does not recognize the request method and is not capable of supporting it for any resource.
when_to_use: Feature not yet available in this API version

example_response.message: This feature is not yet implemented

codes.best_practice: Use 501 for features on the roadmap but not yet implemented. Return an estimated release date if possible. Avoid 501 in production APIs.

codes.title: Bad Gateway
codes.short_description: Upstream server returned an invalid response.
codes.description: The server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from an upstream server it accessed when trying to fulfill the request. Common in microservices architectures when a downstream service fails.

example_response.message: Failed to connect to upstream service

codes.best_practice: Include which upstream service failed. Implement circuit breakers. Use health checks to remove unhealthy nodes from the pool automatically.

codes.title: Service Unavailable
codes.short_description: Server temporarily unable to handle the request.
codes.description: The server is not ready to handle the request. Common causes are a server that is down for maintenance or that is overloaded. A Retry-After header should be sent to indicate when the service is expected to be available again.

example_response.message: Service is under maintenance

codes.best_practice: Return Retry-After with an RFC 7231 date. Serve 503 from a separate health check endpoint. Use circuit breakers to automatically serve 503 when downstream failures spike.

codes.title: Gateway Timeout
codes.short_description: Upstream server did not respond in time.
codes.description: The server, while acting as a gateway or proxy, did not receive a timely response from an upstream server it needed to access to complete the request. This is different from 408 Request Timeout, which is about the client timing out.

example_response.message: Upstream service did not respond within 30 seconds

codes.best_practice: Set aggressive timeouts on all downstream calls. Use async patterns for long-running operations. Never wait indefinitely for any external service.

codes.title: HTTP Version Not Supported
codes.short_description: HTTP version used in request is not supported.
codes.description: The server does not support or refuses to support the major version of HTTP that was used in the request message. The server is indicating that it is unable or unwilling to complete the request using the same major version as the client.
when_to_use: Security policy rejecting old HTTP versions

example_response.message: HTTP/1.0 is not supported. Please use HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.

codes.best_practice: Enforce HTTP/1.1 minimum in modern APIs. Prefer HTTP/2 for performance. Never support HTTP/1.0 in new APIs due to security limitations.

codes.title: Variant Also Negotiates
codes.short_description: Server has a configuration error in content negotiation.
codes.description: The server has an internal configuration error: the chosen variant resource is configured to engage in transparent content negotiation itself, and is therefore not a proper endpoint in the negotiation process.

example_response.message: Server configuration error in content negotiation

codes.best_practice: This indicates a server misconfiguration. Fix the content negotiation configuration so the variant resource does not itself negotiate.

codes.title: Insufficient Storage
codes.short_description: Server cannot store the representation needed (WebDAV).
codes.description: The method could not be performed on the resource because the server is unable to store the representation needed to successfully complete the request. This condition is considered to be temporary.

example_response.message: Storage quota exceeded

codes.best_practice: Monitor disk usage and alert before hitting limits. Implement storage quotas per user or tenant. Return current and max storage in the response.

codes.title: Loop Detected
codes.short_description: Infinite loop detected while processing request (WebDAV).
codes.description: The server terminated an operation because it encountered an infinite loop while processing a request with Depth: infinity. This status indicates that the entire operation failed.
when_to_use: WebDAV COPY/MOVE operations with circular references

example_response.message: Circular reference detected in the directory structure

codes.best_practice: Track visited resources with a set during recursive operations. Set a maximum recursion depth to prevent stack overflows.

codes.title: Not Extended
codes.short_description: Further extensions to the request are required.
codes.description: The policy for accessing the resource has not been met in the request. The server should send back all the information necessary for the client to issue an extended request. This is used for the HTTP Extension Framework.

example_response.message: The mandatory extension is required for this request

codes.best_practice: Rarely used in modern APIs. Prefer explicit versioning or feature negotiation headers over the HTTP Extension Framework.

codes.title: Network Authentication Required
codes.short_description: Client must authenticate to gain network access.
codes.description: The 511 status code indicates that the client needs to authenticate to gain network access. The response SHOULD contain a link to a resource that allows the user to submit credentials (e.g., a captive portal login page).

example_response.message: You must sign in to access the network

codes.best_practice: Include the login page URL in the response. This code is intended for network infrastructure (captive portals), not application-level auth.

codes.title: Web Server Returns an Unknown Error
codes.short_description: Origin server returned an unexpected response (Cloudflare).
codes.description: The 520 error is used as a catch-all response when the origin server returns something unexpected or an empty, unmapped, or not supported response to Cloudflare. This is a Cloudflare-specific status code.
when_to_use: Empty or malformed response from origin

example_response.error: Web Server Returns an Unknown Error
example_response.message: The origin server returned an unknown error

codes.best_practice: Check your origin server logs. The origin is returning an empty or unexpected response. Common culprit: application crash or missing response handlers.

codes.title: Web Server Is Down
codes.short_description: Origin server refused the connection (Cloudflare).
codes.description: The origin server has refused the connection from Cloudflare. This Cloudflare-specific error occurs when the origin web server is offline or actively refusing connections from Cloudflare's IP ranges.
when_to_use: Origin web server process is stopped

example_response.message: Cloudflare cannot connect to the origin server

codes.best_practice: Ensure your origin server allows connections from all Cloudflare IP ranges. Check server process status and firewall rules.

codes.title: Connection Timed Out
codes.short_description: Cloudflare timed out waiting for the origin server.
codes.description: Cloudflare was able to complete a TCP connection to the origin server, but the origin did not reply with an HTTP response before the connection timed out. This is a Cloudflare-specific status code.
when_to_use: Network congestion between Cloudflare and origin

example_response.message: The connection to the origin server timed out

codes.best_practice: Optimize slow origin responses. Use Cloudflare's timeout settings. For long operations, return 202 Accepted and process asynchronously.

codes.title: Origin Is Unreachable
codes.short_description: Cloudflare cannot reach the origin server (DNS failure).
codes.description: Cloudflare could not reach the origin server. This is typically a DNS resolution failure or the origin server has an incorrect IP address configured in Cloudflare's DNS settings.
when_to_use: Origin IP changed but DNS not updated
Origin server removed without updating Cloudflare

example_response.message: Cloudflare cannot reach the origin server

codes.best_practice: Verify your DNS settings in Cloudflare. Ensure the origin IP is correct and reachable. Check for DNS propagation issues after IP changes.

codes.title: A Timeout Occurred
codes.short_description: Cloudflare established a connection but origin timed out.
codes.description: Cloudflare was able to connect to the origin server but the connection timed out before the origin server sent a complete response. Different from 522, as the TCP connection was established.
when_to_use: Origin took too long to respond
Database query ran longer than 100 seconds
PHP/Node process timed out on origin

example_response.message: The origin server timed out after establishing a connection

codes.best_practice: For operations exceeding 100 seconds, use streaming responses or return 202 with a polling endpoint. Optimize long-running queries and background jobs.

codes.title: SSL Handshake Failed
codes.short_description: Cloudflare and origin could not complete an SSL handshake.
codes.description: Cloudflare could not negotiate a SSL/TLS handshake with the origin server. This typically happens when the origin server's SSL certificate is misconfigured or incompatible with Cloudflare's SSL modes.
when_to_use: Self-signed cert without Cloudflare Full SSL mode

example_response.message: Cloudflare cannot complete the SSL handshake with the origin

codes.best_practice: Ensure your origin server has a valid SSL certificate. For Cloudflare Full (strict) mode, use a certificate signed by a trusted CA. Keep TLS version at 1.2+.

codes.title: Invalid SSL Certificate
codes.short_description: Cloudflare could not validate the origin SSL certificate.
codes.description: Cloudflare could not validate the SSL certificate on the origin web server. This occurs specifically in 'Full (Strict)' SSL mode when the origin certificate is self-signed, expired, or otherwise untrusted.
when_to_use: Self-signed certificate on origin in Full Strict mode

example_response.message: The origin's SSL certificate could not be validated

codes.best_practice: Install a valid SSL certificate from a recognized CA on your origin. Use Cloudflare's Origin Certificate for free automatic certificate management.

codes.title: No Response
codes.short_description: Server returns no information and closes the connection (Nginx).
codes.description: A non-standard status code used by Nginx to instruct the server to return no information to the client and close the connection immediately. Often used to deter malicious or bot traffic by refusing to serve a response.
when_to_use: Blocking known bad IPs or bots

example_response.message: Connection closed without response

codes.best_practice: Use 444 in Nginx at the server block level to silently drop connections from known bad actors. More resource-efficient than 403 since no response is sent.

codes.title: Client Closed Request
codes.short_description: Client closed the connection before server could respond (Nginx).
codes.description: A non-standard status code introduced by Nginx for the case when the client closes the connection while Nginx was still processing the request. Useful for logging and monitoring request abandonment.

example_response.message: The client disconnected before the server could complete the response

codes.best_practice: Monitor 499 rates in your logs. High 499 rates indicate slow responses. Implement streaming, faster APIs, or request cancellation handling on the server.
